newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila swallows bitter pill; is the ailment cured?.
newsitem.headline: Manila swallows bitter pill; is the ailment cured?.

text.p: Exporters heralded the recent de facto devaluation of the Philippine peso, saying it was a bitter pill that would finally put to rest nagging concerns over the widening current account deficit.

While it cheapens the price of locally-manufactured goods in the world market and discourages massive imports, leading economists said a weak peso is not the final solution to the thorny issue of trade imbalance.

"It's not the issue of pricing that is creating the trade deficit. We import a lot of our exports. Our number one import is our number one export," Johnny Noe Ravalo, chief economist of the BAP Policy Research Group, told Reuters.

Philippine exporters rely heavily on imported components to manufacture their products. The country's biggest dollar-earners are the electronics and computer-related manufacturers who import the components from Japan and the United States.
"We have very little intermediate industries. We tend to import cheap and put in a little value-added and export it out again," Ravalo said.
In a global economy, such an economic structure is not likely to survive in the long term since many other countries can easily reproduce the same product with cheaper labour, he added.

Asian Institute of Management (AIM) president Felipe Alfonso agreed, saying lagging labour productivity might spell trouble in the longer term with workers in other Asian countries producing more for lower wages.
He said a major shift into skills-oriented industries, such as software programming and other services sectors, should be promoted to extricate the country from its import-export cycle.
The current account deficit, estimated at about five to six percent of the gross domestic product (GDP), has drawn disparate views regarding the real status of the economy.
Some economists warned it was a sign of fundamental flaws in the basic economic structure, while others said it was inevitable, or even a necessary evil, for an industrialising economy.
It was the former view which put the peso under incessant speculative pressure in recent months, as many foreign fund managers bet that Asia's newest economic star would be the next to fade.
The question is now whether the prevailing low inflation and high growth will hold after the de facto devaluation.
Emilio Neri, a senior economist at the University of Asia and the Pacific, said an economic slowdown is inevitable.
"The overall trend of an upward growth over the medium term will continue, but short-term adjustment is inevitable. I expect flat growth, or even a deceleration, in the economy this year," Neri said.
He said the high interest rates, which preceded the sharp peso depreciation, and uncertainties which followed the fall, will slow down investment plans.
BAP's Ravalo welcomed the respite after five years of accelerating growth.
"Nineteen ninety-seven and 1998 will be the consolidation years. We should not be worried at all. It's a healthy and expected consolidation," he said.
Felipe Medalla, dean of the University of the Philippines' School of Economics, said: "It was a choice between slowdown and a freefall."
But economists said the country's low savings rate, sluggish manufacturing and low labour productivity still hobbled the economy.
Taxation still needed reform while bottlenecks in infrastructure threatened to limit expansion.
On top of all that, there is a danger that in the run-up to next May's presidential election the government might be tempted to backpedal on some economic reforms.
The true value of the peso might have been found last week, but the panacea for the economic shortcomings remained elusive, they said.
